newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ bank bill rates fall as TWI climbs 30 points.
newsitem.headline: NZ bank bill rates fall as TWI climbs 30 points.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD
OVERNIGHT CASH 9.15 PCT (PREV 9.35) US 5-YR 5.84 (PREV 5.84)
* NZ money market boosted at close by strong TWI
* Market bullish as Reserve Bank's December MPS looms
* Hopes pinned on government formation soon
The New Zealand money market enjoyed a strong finish on Tuesday, helped along by a 30 point rally in the currency's Trade Weighted Index to 67.40.
"It's just a continuing combination of all positive factors and no negatives," one bill dealer said.
He said the market was bulled up ahead of the Reserve Bank's Monetary Policy Statement on December 17, in which it expects a formal condoning of easier monetary conditions.

"Obviously the Reserve Bank is happy with conditions easing slightly, because they've allowed them to do so without saying anything. I guess the market will just keep rallying until they get an indication from the Reserve Bank that things have gone too far."

The 90-days shed eight basis points on the day to 8.38 percent, while the December futures contract climbed seven points to 91.75. Cash remained at 9.15 percent after its move down from 9.35 percent on Monday, and dealers expect it to stay there until they hear what the RBNZ has to say on the 17th.
Bonds had a quieter day and ended largely flat, although the 11/06 broke below its earlier low of 6.95 percent, which dealers said cleared the way for a move to 6.89 percent.

The market is hoping New Zealand will have a new government either late this week or by early next week, and dealers said the market had priced in "to a large degree" a coalition deal between the caretaker National Party government and nationalist New Zealand First.
Any rally on such a deal would not be huge and was likely to be fairly short lived.
NZ First has been negotiating with both National and the centre-left Labour Party over the shape of the new government, following October 12's inconclusive general election.
